questions.stem: According to legend, Rome was founded in 753 BCE by:
options: Julius Caesar, after his great victory over the Gauls
Remus, who named the new city after his own family
Romulus, who killed his twin brother Remus in a quarrel
Aeneas, who had escaped by ship from the burning city of Troy
questions.explanation: In the legend the twins Romulus and Remus were abandoned, suckled by a she-wolf and raised by a shepherd; Romulus killed Remus in a quarrel over the new city and named it after himself. Aeneas, a Trojan prince, was said to be their ancestor who had reached Italy centuries earlier. Julius Caesar lived about 700 years after the legendary founding date.

questions.stem: In Virgil's Aeneid, written in the time of Augustus, the hero Aeneas is:
options: a Greek king who led the army that captured and destroyed Troy
the shepherd who found and raised the twins Romulus and Remus
the first emperor of Rome, who brought peace after the civil wars
a Trojan prince who escaped Troy and whose descendants founded Rome
questions.explanation: Virgil's epic linked Rome to the heroic world of Troy and presented the Romans as destined to rule; Augustus' family, the Julii, claimed descent from Aeneas' son. The shepherd who raised the twins was Faustulus, and the first emperor was Augustus himself, who encouraged Virgil's work. Myths like this gave Rome and its rulers prestige.

questions.stem: Why was the site of Rome well placed for a city to grow?
options: It lay at the mouth of the Po, the longest river in all of Italy
It controlled the only pass through the Alps into the rest of Europe
It sat on defensible hills by a crossing of the Tiber, near the sea
It stood right on the coast, around a large natural harbour for warships
questions.explanation: Rome's hills offered protection, the Tiber provided water and a route to the sea about 25 kilometres away, and an island and ford made the spot a natural crossing on trade routes through central Italy, surrounded by fertile plains. The city was inland, using the port of Ostia at the Tiber's mouth. The Po flows across northern Italy, far from Rome.

questions.stem: In the Roman Republic, what were the consuls?
options: Kings who ruled for life and chose their own heirs
Priests who read the will of the gods in omens
Officials elected only by plebeians to protect them
Two elected leaders who shared power for one year
questions.explanation: After expelling their last king, traditionally in 509 BCE, the Romans created a Republic with two consuls elected each year, so that no single person held power for long; each could block the other. The Senate, made up of former officials, advised them and controlled finances. Officials elected by plebeians to protect their interests were the tribunes.

questions.stem: In the early Roman Republic, who were the patricians?
options: Freed slaves who had been given Roman citizenship
Foreign merchants who lived in the city of Rome but were not citizens
Members of old, wealthy families who held most political power
Ordinary citizens such as farmers, traders and craftsmen
questions.explanation: Patricians were a small group of aristocratic families who at first controlled the Senate, the priesthoods and the consulship. Most citizens were plebeians, who struggled for about two centuries in the Conflict of the Orders until they could hold every office. Freed slaves were known as freedmen and freedwomen.

questions.stem: During the Conflict of the Orders, plebeians won the right to elect tribunes. What power did a tribune have?
options: To veto actions of officials that harmed plebeians
To command all of Rome's legions in a time of foreign war
To appoint new senators who served for life
To rule alone as dictator in an emergency
questions.explanation: Tribunes, chosen only by plebeians, could say 'veto' ('I forbid') to stop an official's action or a law that harmed plebeians, and harming a tribune was a serious religious crime. Plebeians won this by refusing to work or fight until the patricians gave way. The Twelve Tables, Rome's first written laws, were another early plebeian gain.

questions.stem: Where did most slaves in the Roman Republic come from?
options: Volunteers who signed up for a fixed number of years
Prisoners captured in Rome's wars of conquest
Citizens who could not pay their yearly taxes
Criminals sentenced to slavery by the Senate
questions.explanation: Rome's wars brought in huge numbers of captives, who worked on farms, in mines, in households and as gladiators. Slaves were legally property, but many were freed by their owners and became freedmen and freedwomen, whose children could be full citizens. Enslaving Roman citizens for debt was abolished early in the Republic.

questions.stem: Spartacus led a huge slave revolt against Rome in 73–71 BCE. Who was he?
options: A general from Carthage
A Christian leader in Judaea
A gladiator from Thrace
A Roman senator who freed his slaves
questions.explanation: Spartacus, a Thracian trained as a gladiator at Capua, broke out with a small group and built an army of tens of thousands of escaped slaves that defeated several Roman forces. Crassus finally crushed the revolt, and about 6,000 captured rebels were crucified along the Appian Way. Christianity did not begin until the following century.

questions.stem: The Carthaginian general Hannibal is famous for:
options: defeating Julius Caesar in the civil war that began in 49 BCE
building a wall across northern Britain to stop raiders
leading an army with elephants over the Alps into Italy
sacking the city of Rome and ending the Western Empire
questions.explanation: In the Second Punic War Hannibal crossed the Alps in 218 BCE and won great victories such as Cannae, but Rome refused to surrender and defeated him at Zama in 202 BCE. The three Punic Wars (264–146 BCE) ended with Carthage destroyed and Rome dominant in the western Mediterranean. Rome was sacked much later, by the Visigoths in 410 CE.

questions.stem: From around 107 BCE, Gaius Marius recruited landless poor citizens as paid, professional soldiers. How did this help bring about the fall of the Republic?
options: Soldiers were banned from voting, so the assemblies lost their power
Soldiers became loyal to the generals who paid them, not to the Senate
The army became too small to defend Rome against its foreign enemies
Slaves replaced citizens in the legions, and the army soon rebelled
questions.explanation: Marius' soldiers depended on their general for pay, loot and land when they retired, so ambitious commanders such as Sulla and later Julius Caesar could lead armies against Rome itself. The reforms made the legions more professional and effective, not smaller, and slaves were not normally allowed to serve. Civil wars between generals followed in the next decades.

questions.stem: In 49 BCE Julius Caesar led his army across the Rubicon river. Why was this so significant?
options: It was the border of Gaul, which he then went on to conquer
It marked Rome's final victory over Carthage in the Punic Wars
He was crowned as Rome's first emperor on the river's banks
Bringing an army into Italy was illegal, so it began a civil war
questions.explanation: The Rubicon marked the edge of Caesar's province, and a general could not lawfully bring troops into Italy, so crossing it was a declaration of war on the Senate and his rival Pompey. Caesar had already conquered Gaul over the previous decade. 'Crossing the Rubicon' still means taking a step that cannot be undone.

questions.stem: Julius Caesar was assassinated on the Ides of March, 44 BCE, by:
options: rebel gladiators who had escaped from Capua
senators who feared he meant to rule as a king
his adopted heir Octavian, who wanted power himself
Cleopatra's bodyguards, sent from Alexandria
questions.explanation: Caesar had been made dictator for life, and a group of senators led by Brutus and Cassius stabbed him at a meeting of the Senate, claiming to defend the Republic. Instead more civil wars followed, which his great-nephew and adopted heir Octavian eventually won. Octavian avenged Caesar rather than plotting against him.

questions.stem: Who became Rome's first emperor, taking the name Augustus in 27 BCE?
options: Octavian
Julius Caesar
Mark Antony
Nero
questions.explanation: Octavian defeated Mark Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BCE and in 27 BCE received the title Augustus, keeping the outward forms of the Republic while holding real power. Julius Caesar is often mistaken for the first emperor, but he was a dictator who was killed before the empire was formally established. Nero ruled later, from 54 to 68 CE.

questions.stem: What was the Pax Romana?
options: About 200 years of relative peace in the empire, starting with Augustus
The treaty that ended the Punic Wars between Rome and Carthage
The great paved road that linked the city of Rome to the port of Brundisium
The oath of loyalty that every legionary swore to the Roman Senate
questions.explanation: The 'Roman Peace' lasted from Augustus to about the death of Marcus Aurelius in 180 CE, a time when trade, roads and cities grew across the empire, although wars still took place on the frontiers and revolts were crushed. The road to Brundisium was the Appian Way.

questions.stem: Why are Pompeii and Herculaneum such valuable evidence of Roman daily life?
options: Their people kept diaries that describe every part of their daily lives
They were never abandoned, so families still live in the same houses
The emperor rebuilt them exactly as they had been after a great fire
Vesuvius buried them suddenly in 79 CE, preserving homes and objects
questions.explanation: Volcanic ash and pumice buried Pompeii, and hot volcanic flows buried Herculaneum, sealing houses, shops, paintings, graffiti, food and even the shapes of victims. Archaeologists can therefore see ordinary life frozen at a single moment. Pliny the Younger's letters give an eyewitness account of the eruption.

questions.stem: What were the lares in a Roman household?
options: Slaves who did the cooking and cleaning for the family
Dining rooms where the family entertained its guests
Lead pipes that brought water in from the aqueduct
Guardian spirits honoured at a shrine in the home
questions.explanation: Each home had a lararium, a small shrine where the family offered food, wine and prayers to the lares and other household gods, led by the father as head of the household. Religion was part of daily family life as well as of public temples and festivals. The dining room was the triclinium.

questions.stem: Where were chariot races held in ancient Rome?
options: The Forum
The Pantheon
The Circus Maximus
The Colosseum
questions.explanation: The Circus Maximus, a long racetrack that could hold more than 150,000 spectators, hosted chariot races between teams such as the Blues and the Greens. The Colosseum, an amphitheatre opened in 80 CE, held gladiator fights and animal hunts. The Forum was Rome's political and business centre, and the Pantheon a temple.

questions.stem: How did Roman aqueducts carry water into cities?
options: Using pumps driven by teams of slaves turning large wooden wheels
Using steam engines to push the water through lead pipes
Using the force of the ocean tides to drive water inland
Using a gentle, steady downhill slope over many kilometres
questions.explanation: Aqueducts used gravity: engineers built channels, tunnels and arched bridges that dropped very slightly along their whole length, bringing fresh water from the hills to fountains, baths and homes. With roads and concrete, which made domes like the Pantheon's possible, they are among Rome's most lasting legacies. Steam power was not used until about 1,700 years later.

questions.stem: Why were Christians sometimes persecuted in the Roman Empire before 313 CE?
options: They worshipped Isis, whose cult was the only one Rome banned
They refused to worship the Roman gods and honour the emperor
They refused to pay any taxes at all to the Roman government
They had fought on the side of Carthage in the wars against Rome
questions.explanation: Romans accepted many foreign gods, such as Isis and Mithras, as long as people also took part in the state cults, but Christians worshipped only one God and would not sacrifice to the gods or the emperor, which looked like disloyalty. Emperors such as Nero and Diocletian ordered persecutions, though these were not constant. Christianity kept spreading through the cities of the empire.

questions.stem: What did the Edict of Milan, agreed in 313 CE under Constantine, do?
options: Banned gladiator fights in every city of the empire
Allowed freedom of worship, ending persecution of Christians
Made Christianity the only legal religion of the empire
Divided the empire permanently into eastern and western halves
questions.explanation: Constantine, who had come to favour Christianity, and his co-emperor Licinius granted religious toleration to Christians and others, and returned confiscated church property. Christianity became the official religion only later, under Theodosius I in 380 CE. The edict is often wrongly remembered as making Christianity the state religion.

questions.stem: Under which emperor did the Roman Empire reach its greatest size, around 117 CE?
options: Trajan
Augustus
Hadrian
Constantine
questions.explanation: Trajan's conquests of Dacia and, briefly, Mesopotamia took the empire to its greatest extent, from Britain to the Persian Gulf. His successor Hadrian gave up some eastern conquests and built fixed frontiers, including Hadrian's Wall across northern Britain from 122 CE. Augustus expanded the empire greatly, but not as far as Trajan.

questions.stem: How did Rome and Han China mainly know about each other?
options: Through embassies sent between the two emperors every single year
Through a long war fought along the border the two empires shared
Through Roman merchants who settled and lived in the Han capital
Through goods such as silk passed between many traders on the Silk Road
questions.explanation: Silk reached Rome through Parthian, Indian and other middlemen, and the Roman writer Florus mentions envoys from the Seres, the 'silk people', but there was little direct contact. Chinese records describe a group claiming to come from the Roman emperor reaching the Han court in 166 CE. The two empires never shared a border.

questions.stem: The Western Roman Empire is usually said to have ended in 476 CE when:
options: Constantine moved the empire's capital from Rome to Byzantium
the Germanic leader Odoacer removed the last western emperor
Mount Vesuvius erupted and destroyed the city of Rome itself
the Ottoman Turks captured the great city of Constantinople
questions.explanation: Odoacer deposed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus and did not replace him, a date historians use to mark the end of Roman rule in the west after decades of invasions, civil wars and economic strain. The Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire lasted almost another thousand years, until the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453. Constantine founded Constantinople much earlier, in 330 CE.

questions.stem: Agrippina the Younger is remembered as a powerful Roman woman who:
options: led a great revolt of the Britons against the Roman army in Britain
ruled Egypt as its last queen and allied herself with Mark Antony
ruled the empire alone as the first woman to be named emperor
helped her son Nero become emperor and influenced his early reign
questions.explanation: Agrippina, a great-granddaughter of Augustus, married the emperor Claudius and secured the succession for her son Nero, then shared in power during his first years until he had her killed in 59 CE. Her career shows how elite Roman women could exercise power through family, even though they could not hold office. The revolt in Britain was led by Boudica, and Egypt's last queen was Cleopatra VII.

questions.stem: Marcus Aurelius, emperor from 161 to 180 CE, is best remembered for:
options: conquering Britain and adding it to the empire for the first time
becoming the first Roman emperor to convert to Christianity
his Meditations, a book of Stoic philosophy written on campaign
building the Colosseum to hold gladiator games for the people
questions.explanation: Marcus Aurelius spent much of his reign fighting on the Danube frontier and wrote private reflections on duty, self-control and accepting fate, later published as the Meditations. The Colosseum was built under Vespasian and Titus, Britain was invaded under Claudius in 43 CE, and Constantine was the first Christian emperor.
